summary: Kerak, east of the Dead Sea: the castle Pagan the Butler began about 1142 as the seat of the crusader lordship of Oultrejordain, Reynald of Châtillon's base, besieged by Saladin in 1183 and 1184 and surrendered in 1188, then an Ayyubid treasury and a Mamluk fortress where deposed sultans, Baraka Khan among them, were kept.
overview: Kerak was the chief castle of Oultrejordain, the crusader barony east of the Jordan, and it sat across the road joining Egypt to Syria and the pilgrim road to Mecca. It resisted Saladin twice before surrendering in 1188, then served the Ayyubids as a treasury and princely seat and the Mamluks as a provincial fortress, a prison for Baraka Khan and a refuge for sultans waiting to reclaim the throne.
knownFor: Seat of the crusader lordship of Oultrejordain, begun by Pagan the Butler about 1142
Base of Reynald of Châtillon's caravan raids and his Red Sea expedition of 1182–1183
Besieged by Saladin during the wedding of Isabella I of Jerusalem and Humphrey IV of Toron in 1183
Surrendered to Saladin's troops in 1188 after a blockade of about eighteen months
Mamluk fortress where Baraka Khan died in exile and al-Nasir Ahmad held out until 1344

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Kerak stands at the southern tip of a plateau east of the Dead Sea, ringed by deep valleys and cut off from its town by a rock-cut ditch. The Franks called it Crac, or Crac des Moabites, and Arabic writers al-Karak. From about 1142 it was the seat of the lords of Oultrejordain, whose barony straddled the caravan road between Damascus and Egypt.

It held out against Saladin in 1183 and 1184 and fell to his troops only after Hattin had removed any hope of relief. Under the Ayyubids and Mamluks it became a treasury, a princely seat and a place to keep inconvenient rulers: Baraka Khan died there in exile, and deposed sultans used it to wait out their rivals until 1390.

contentSections.title: Moab and Charachmoba
paragraphs: The plateau lay in Iron Age Moab, and the town is traditionally identified with Kir-hareseth, the Moabite stronghold of the Books of Kings; its later name comes from the Aramaic karka, 'town'. After the Roman annexation of the Nabataean kingdom in 106 it belonged to the province of Arabia. The sixth-century Madaba mosaic map shows it as Charachmoba, a walled town on a height, and its bishop Demetrius attended a council at Jerusalem in 536.

Muslim armies first met Byzantine frontier troops in 629 at Mu'tah, which Abu al-Fida placed a day's march from Kerak, and the tomb of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib there was still visited in his time. Under the caliphs the town is barely recorded, but it kept many Christians: Syriac Christian farmers and shepherds sheltered in the town when Saladin arrived in 1183.

contentSections.title: Pagan the Butler and the new castle, about 1142
paragraphs: Baldwin I of Jerusalem built Montreal, far to the south, in 1115 or 1116 to watch the caravan road. By 1126 the barony around it belonged to Pagan the Butler, named as butler to Baldwin II of Jerusalem in 1120; Hans Eberhard Mayer argued that the butler and the lord of Montreal were different men, a view other historians have not followed.

About 1142, late in King Fulk's reign, Pagan moved his seat north to the plateau above the Wadi al-Karak, nearer the Dead Sea and Jerusalem, and began the castle that Latin writers also called Petra Deserti. One modern explanation links the move to a raid from Syria across the Jordan that Montreal had failed to stop. Pagan died in the late 1140s and his nephew Maurice succeeded him.

contentSections.title: The lordship of Oultrejordain, 1161–1177
paragraphs: Oultrejordain had no fixed eastern frontier: it ran from the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba and faded into the desert along the pilgrim road. The thirteenth-century jurist John of Ibelin counted it among the four great baronies of the kingdom. Its wealth lay in the wheat, olives and pomegranates of the plateau, salt from the Dead Sea and tolls on the caravans.

On 31 July 1161 Philip of Milly gave his lordship of Nablus to Baldwin III of Jerusalem in exchange for Oultrejordain, though the king kept the caravan and Bedouin tolls. Philip strengthened Kerak with a ditch and towers, and in 1165 or 1166 he joined the Knights Templar, handing part of the lordship to the order, which he led as grand master from 1169 to 1171.

The barony then passed through his daughters. Stephanie of Milly lost her first husband, Humphrey III of Toron, about 1173, and her second, Miles of Plancy, was murdered in 1174. In 1176 or 1177 Baldwin IV of Jerusalem gave her in marriage to Reynald of Châtillon, lately ransomed after about fifteen years as a prisoner in Aleppo.

contentSections.title: Reynald of Châtillon and the Red Sea, 1177–1183
paragraphs: A charter of November 1177 is the first to style Reynald lord of Hebron and Montreal, and he owed the crown sixty knights. From Kerak he sat across the road joining the two halves of Saladin's empire. The chronicler Ernoul records two attacks on caravans in time of truce, and late in 1181 or early in 1182 Reynald rode as far as Tabuk on the road to Mecca.

In the winter of 1182–1183 he had at least five ships built in Oultrejordain and carried by camel across the Negev to the Gulf of Aqaba. The Franks took Ayla and blockaded the Egyptian fort on Pharaoh's Island while the rest of the flotilla attacked ships carrying pilgrims and goods along the Arabian coast, within reach of Mecca and Medina.

Saladin's brother al-Adil, governor of Egypt, launched a fleet on the Red Sea that relieved the island and trapped the raiders near al-Hawra. Reynald had already gone home. Saladin ordered the captives killed in cities across his lands, by one Arabic account two of them at Mina during the pilgrimage, and the Andalusian traveller Ibn Jubayr, landing at Alexandria in March 1183, saw Frankish prisoners brought in on camels.

contentSections.title: Saladin's sieges, 1183–1188
paragraphs: In the autumn of 1183 Kerak was crowded for the wedding of Reynald's stepson, Humphrey IV of Toron, to Isabella I of Jerusalem, Baldwin IV's eleven-year-old half-sister, who had lived at Kerak since their betrothal in 1180. Saladin left Damascus on 22 October and closed on Kerak in November; al-Adil joined him with the Egyptian army on 22 November. The defenders abandoned the town the next day, and by Ernoul's account Reynald reached the castle only because one of his men held the bridge over the ditch.

William of Tyre, then chancellor of the kingdom, says six trebuchets in the town battered the north front and two more stood on a ridge to the south; Ibn al-Athir counts seven. The stones could not break the walls. Ernoul, who probably had the story from the bride's mother, Queen Maria, says Stephanie sent dishes from the feast out to Saladin, and he asked which tower the couple slept in and had his engineers spare it.

The news forced a decision in Jerusalem. Baldwin IV dismissed Guy of Lusignan as regent, had his nephew crowned co-king as Baldwin V on 20 November, and, blind and carried in a litter, went with the army to the Dead Sea before handing command to Raymond III of Tripoli. Saladin, who had sent his Egyptian troops home, lifted the siege on 3 December, and the royal army entered Kerak the next day.

Saladin returned in the summer of 1184 and tried to fill the northern ditch so that his engines could reach the wall, but withdrew after about four weeks as the royal army approached. In 1187 Reynald was captured at Hattin and killed by Saladin himself. Stephanie offered Kerak and Montreal for the release of her son Humphrey, but the garrisons refused her order. Blockaded since the spring of 1187, Kerak surrendered on terms, by the usual dating in November 1188, and Montreal early in 1189.

contentSections.title: Ayyubid Kerak, 1188–1263
paragraphs: Kerak passed to al-Adil, who kept one of his treasuries there, and it remained a treasury of the dynasty. The geographer Yaqut, who died in 1229, called it a very strongly fortified castle on a rock surrounded by wadis except on the side towards the suburb. It later formed part of the lands of al-Adil's son al-Mu'azzam Isa, prince of Damascus, who by one account had a tunnel cut from the castle into the town in 1227.

Al-Mu'azzam's son al-Nasir Dawud lost Damascus to his uncles al-Ashraf and al-Kamil, who besieged him there until 25 June 1229, and kept Kerak as compensation. In 1239 his cousin as-Salih Ayyub, driven from Damascus, fell into his hands and was held at Kerak. That December Dawud took Jerusalem from the Franks and pulled down its defences, and in April 1240 he released Ayyub and went with him to Cairo, where Ayyub became sultan.

Ayyub later turned on him: Dawud lost his lands west of the Jordan in 1245 and was deposed in 1248, and Kerak passed to Ayyub in 1249. After the Mamluks seized Egypt in 1250, al-Mughith Umar, a son of the Ayyubid sultan al-Adil II, ruled Kerak and Shawbak as an independent prince, and in the late 1250s the exiled Bahri mamluks, Baybars among them, used his lands as a base against Egypt.

contentSections.title: Baybars and the Mamluk province, 1263–1286
paragraphs: As sultan, Baybars would not leave an independent Ayyubid fortress on the pilgrim road. Accusing al-Mughith of dealings with the Mongols, he had him arrested and killed in 1263, and al-Mughith's sons surrendered Kerak and the other castles of southern Jordan. Baybars installed a governor and garrison and rebuilt the defences; the Karak Resources Project attributes the towers called Burj al-Zahir and Burj al-Banawi to his work.

Kerak became the seat of a Mamluk province whose governors also held Shawbak by the fourteenth century. Baybars' secretary Ibn Abd al-Zahir wrote that the castle housed four government offices, for the army, finance, Kerak itself and the chancery. Al-Dimashqi, who died in 1327, called it an impregnable fortress whose ditches were the valleys around it, 'a treasure house of the Turks'.

contentSections.title: A prison and a refuge for sultans, 1279–1390
paragraphs: Baraka Khan succeeded Baybars in 1277 and tried to replace his father's senior emirs with his own mamluks. In 1279 Qalawun and the great emirs forced him to abdicate in favour of his seven-year-old brother Sulamish and sent him to Kerak, where his brother Khadir joined him. Baraka died there in 1280, of illness or, by one account, a fall from his horse, and was buried in Damascus in the Zahiriyya, the mausoleum he had built for his father. An inscription added there under Qalawun dates his funeral to the Islamic year 680, which began in April 1281 and sits awkwardly with the usual date.

Khadir, styled al-Malik al-Mas'ud by Qalawun in 1280 for his holding of Kerak, kept the castle until 1286, when Qalawun took it under direct rule. Qalawun's son al-Nasir Muhammad, set aside as a boy in 1294, lived at Kerak until his recall to the throne in 1299. In 1309, weary of the regents who ruled in his name, he announced a pilgrimage, went to Kerak instead and abdicated; the next year he marched on Cairo with Syrian and Bedouin support and reigned until 1341.

His son al-Nasir Ahmad grew up largely at Kerak. Proclaimed sultan in January 1342, he left Cairo for Kerak by the end of May with treasury money, his father's horses and senior officials. Deposed that June, he held the fortress with the townspeople and nearby Bedouin through seven or eight sieges, the count differing between sources, until defectors showed the besiegers a weak point on 4 July 1344. He was put to death on 16 July and his body buried below the fortress.

In 1389 the governors Mintash and Yalbugha al-Nasiri rose against the sultan Barquq and took Cairo, and Barquq was captured and sent to Kerak. He gathered his supporters from there and was back on the throne in Cairo by February 1390.

contentSections.title: Rulers and notable figures
paragraphs: The Frankish lords of Kerak were Pagan the Butler, his nephew Maurice (to 1161), Philip of Milly (1161 to 1165 or 1166), Philip's daughter Helena with her husband Walter Brisebarre, and Stephanie of Milly with her husbands Humphrey III of Toron, Miles of Plancy and Reynald of Châtillon (1177–1187). Stephanie's son Humphrey IV of Toron kept only the title after 1188.

Its Muslim holders were al-Adil, al-Mu'azzam Isa, al-Nasir Dawud (1229–1248), as-Salih Ayyub and al-Mughith Umar (1250–1263), then Mamluk governors, with Baraka Khan and Khadir, al-Nasir Muhammad, al-Nasir Ahmad and Barquq among its residents. The Christian physician Ibn al-Quff, author of an early Arabic treatise written for surgeons alone, was born at Kerak in 1233.

contentSections.title: The castle
paragraphs: The castle fills the southern end of a plateau about 850 metres long, with the town on the rest. Rock-cut ditches divide it from the town to the north and from a higher ridge to the south, probably the place William of Tyre called Obelet; the southern ditch is said to have doubled as a cistern. The north front carries the best-preserved Frankish work, a thick wall containing two levels of long vaulted halls that served as quarters, stables and stores and as shelter from bombardment.

The towers are rectangular and closely spaced, and a sloping masonry glacis sheathes the steep lower faces. A chapel stands on the east side, about halfway along the curtain wall. By the usual reading of the fabric, the Frankish walls are of roughly shaped volcanic stone and the rebuilding after 1188 used limestone from nearby quarries, both with drafted margins. The lower court on the western side held the site museum until 2019.

contentSections.title: The walled town
paragraphs: Ibn Battuta, who camped outside Kerak with the pilgrim caravan in 1326, called it Hisn al-Ghurab, the Crow's Fortress, and wrote that it had a single gateway, reached through a passage tunnelled in the living rock that formed a kind of hall. Abu al-Fida described a valley below with a bathhouse and gardens of apricots, pears and pomegranates. The Egyptian troops of Ibrahim Pasha damaged the castle when they took it in 1834, local people later dug out stone for saltpetre, and Paul Deschamps and the architect François Anus drew the first accurate plans in 1929.

contentSections.title: Kerak beyond its walls
paragraphs: While Kerak was Frankish, any ruler joining Egypt to Syria had to pass beneath it. Reynald's attacks from the castle on caravans broke the truces of the early 1180s, and his Red Sea fleet brought Frankish raiders within reach of Mecca and Medina for the only time. The surrender of 1188 freed the road from Cairo to Damascus, and the title of lord of Oultrejordain lived on as a claim of Stephanie's descendants, the lords of Toron and Tyre.

For the Mamluks, Kerak's distance from Cairo and its hold on the pilgrim road made it both a secure prison and a dangerous refuge: al-Nasir Muhammad in 1310 and Barquq in 1390 each returned from it to reclaim the throne. Ridley Scott's film Kingdom of Heaven of 2005 staged the siege of 1183 before a gate far grander than the castle's real entrance.

sectionImages.caption: Charachmoba, the Byzantine name for Kerak, drawn as a walled hill town on the sixth-century Madaba mosaic map, photographed in 2023.
sectionImages.creator: Ktiv (photograph); unknown mosaicists of the Madaba Map
sectionImages.date: photograph, 15 October 2023 (of a mosaic of the second half of the sixth century)
sectionImages.note: Modern photograph of the Byzantine mosaic. Only part of the Greek name label survives above the town, and the pale areas around the vignette are where the mosaic is lost. The picture is a conventional town symbol, not a survey of the site, and it predates the crusader castle by nearly six centuries.

sectionImages.caption: The north front of Kerak Castle above its rock-cut ditch, the side Saladin's trebuchets battered in 1183, photographed in 2013.
sectionImages.creator: Dosseman
sectionImages.note: Modern photograph. The metal footbridge at the left is a modern visitors' entrance across the ditch. The wall stands on scarped rock; how much of this face is Frankish and how much was rebuilt after 1188 cannot be told from the photograph alone.

sectionImages.caption: One of the long vaulted halls built into the north side of Kerak Castle, traditionally called the crusaders' stables, photographed in 2020.
sectionImages.creator: Rolfcosar
sectionImages.note: Modern photograph, with modern floor lighting and a gravel path. The photographer's German title calls the hall the crusaders' stables, a traditional name; halls of this kind in the north wall also served as quarters, stores and shelter from bombardment.

sectionImages.caption: A tunnelled entrance to Kerak, photographed by the American Colony Photo Department in Jerusalem between 1898 and 1914.
sectionImages.creator: American Colony Photo Department, Jerusalem
sectionImages.source: Library of Congress, Matson Photograph Collection (matpc.06953), via Wikimedia Commons (public domain)
sectionImages.note: The print is titled '732 Entrance to Kerak'. An arched masonry portal with a panel above it is set into the rock face. Ibn Battuta described the town's entrance as a passage tunnelled through the rock in 1326, but whether this is the passage he used cannot be confirmed from the photograph. The Codex copy is cropped to remove the blank border of the source scan (owner rule: no margins around images).
